claims.text: The overall high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by oxide-layer stability.
A stable oxide layer acts as a protective barrier against wear.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure during deposition enhances formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure during deposition improves wear resistance at elevated temperatures.
The relevant structural mediator is the formation and stability of the oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
The deposition-formed oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during high-temperature wear.
Reduced direct metal-to-metal contact lowers wear at elevated temperatures.
High-temperature oxide stability prevents oxide spallation or degradation.
Preventing oxide spallation or degradation maintains the oxide layer's protective function.
Coatings deposited under increased oxygen partial pressure will have lower wear rates than coatings deposited under standard conditions.
Coatings deposited under increased oxygen partial pressure will lose less material than coatings deposited under standard conditions.
The predicted wear improvement should be particularly evident above 500°C.
The proposed mechanism is applicable from 500°C to 800°C under moderate to high contact loads.
Outside the stated temperature and loading range, oxide-layer stability may not dominate wear behavior.
